panels.description: Whether the last WiFi run's traffic was confirmed, from the interface byte counters, to have left the Wi-Fi interface. en0 and en1 are on the same /25 with the default route on en0, so an ignored bind would measure the wired link and label it WiFi. NOT BOUND means the two tiles to the left are stale - the run was discarded, not published.

panels.description: Step-shaped by design: a textfile gauge holds its value between runs. Wired runs at :00/:30, WiFi at :10/:40, so the two paths are never on the WAN together and the lines are comparable. A WiFi gap is a run whose interface bind could not be proven - see speedtest_bind_ok - not a dead link.

panels.description: Loaded values are interquartile means, so a single outlier cannot move them. WiFi idle latency sitting above wired is the air, not the ISP; WiFi LOADED latency tracking wired is the useful comparison.
panels.title: Idle vs loaded latency

panels.description: Extra delay the link adds once it is saturated - the thing that makes calls and games stutter during a large transfer. Tens of ms is fine, hundreds is a queueing problem at the modem, not a slow link. If both paths bloat by the same amount the queue is upstream of the Mac; if only WiFi does, it is the air.
panels.title: Bufferbloat (loaded minus idle)

panels.description: Wired only - eight extreme-value lines on one panel is unreadable, and the WiFi equivalents are in the WiFi row. The worst-sample lines are single-packet extremes and are routinely 10-100x the IQM. Read them as spike height, not as typical latency.
panels.title: Latency spread (best / worst sample)

panels.description: Wired. Expect ~48 at the half-hourly schedule. The WiFi run has its own ~48 and is not counted here.

panels.description: Wired. A failed run still publishes metrics, so this reads FAILED rather than going blank.

panels.description: Both paths together - this is a quota question, and the WiFi test spends the same quota. Counter, not a sum of the per-run gauges - summing those over time would multiply by the scrape count.

panels.description: Ookla reports 0 far more often than the link is truly lossless; treat any non-zero reading as significant. Loss on WiFi only is a local radio problem; loss on both is the ISP's.
panels.title: Packet loss

panels.description: Non-zero means the speedtest binary errored or returned unparseable output, not that the link was slow. A WiFi run discarded for an unproven bind is NOT a failure - that is speedtest_bind_failures_total, in the WiFi row.
panels.title: Failed runs

panels.description: One row per test path. Identity is kept on this one info metric instead of as labels on the throughput gauges - otherwise changing test server or external IP would start a new series and break every graph above at that point. iface is the single exception, because a second measured path is the one thing that genuinely IS a different series. Interface is what Ookla thought it used; Path is what we bound and verified - they should agree.
